columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Millions of ebooks (fiction, popular, children’s, historical, academic) plus movies, audio, software, and web archives.
Controlled digital lending: one copy per owned physical book; in-copyright works borrowable for 1 hour (browse) or 14 days (full); up to 10 books at a time with a free account.
Public domain works viewable online or downloadable without time limits; some titles need Adobe Digital Editions or compatible apps.
Hachette v. Internet Archive: 500,000+ books removed from general lending; print-disabled access and public domain unchanged.

strengths.title: Huge multi-type digital library
strengths.detail: Ebooks, movies, audio, software, and archived web pages, more than just books.

strengths.title: Controlled digital lending of in-copyright works
strengths.detail: Borrow scanned copies of in-copyright books the Archive has purchased and digitized.

strengths.title: Public domain access and downloads
strengths.detail: Public domain titles can be viewed online or downloaded without time limits.

strengths.title: Free accounts and generous borrowing limits
strengths.detail: Free account; borrow up to 10 ebooks for 14 days each.

weaknesses.title: Borrowing friction and DRM
weaknesses.detail: Many in-copyright titles need Adobe Digital Editions or similar; borrow/return is more complex than consumer stores.

weaknesses.title: Mixed scan quality and metadata
weaknesses.detail: Older scans, OCR errors, and incomplete/inconsistent metadata are common.

weaknesses.title: Legal and access volatility
weaknesses.detail: Hachette case reduced access to many titles; future legal developments could further impact lending.

weaknesses.title: Not optimized for casual reading UX
weaknesses.detail: Library/catalog-oriented UI; reading experience and device sync less polished than Kindle or commercial apps.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Internet Archive / Open Library is nonprofit digital library with Open Library ebook lending, public-domain downloads and controlled digital lending of scanned books. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Internet Archive is a non-profit digital library offering free universal access to books, movies, music, & computer software, as well as 514 billion archived web pages. Official site.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Internet Archive / Open Library side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Internet Archive / Open Library you can use Ebook as a first-class product job. You need a dedicated reader, a giant store, or social tracking of everything you have ever read.

Using Kahana with Internet Archive / Open Library

You can use both. Internet Archive / Open Library keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the reader or tracker you already use. Put the Club pick, discussion questions, and related files on Kahana so the book is a shared library item, not only a private progress bar.
